title: The Lesson I Learned From the Mount of Olives
paragraphs: The Lesson I Learned From the Mount of Olives
There are places in this world that change the way you see a city.
Then there are places that change the way you see yourself.
The Mount of Olives is one of those places.

Standing on its slopes overlooking Jerusalem, it is easy to become captivated by the breathtaking view. The ancient city stretches before your eyes. The golden stones. The winding streets. The history. The promises. The memories.
But the greatest thing about the Mount of Olives is not what you see from it.
It is what happened on it.
And the lesson hidden within its stones may be one of the most life-changing truths a follower of Christ will ever discover.
Because the Mount of Olives is where we learn that God does some of His greatest work in the place between heartbreak and resurrection.
It is where scandal becomes grace.
It is where Jesus rewrites everything.
The mountain appears repeatedly throughout Scripture. King David crossed it while fleeing betrayal from his own son Absalom.
2 Samuel 15:30 tells us:
"David continued up the Mount of Olives, weeping as he went."
The Hebrew text uses the word בֹּכֶה (bokheh), meaning "weeping continuously."
Not a few tears.
Not a momentary sadness.
This was deep grief.
Unrelenting sorrow.
A broken king ascending a mountain with a broken heart.
Centuries later another King would climb the same mountain.
And He would carry an even greater burden.
The Mount of Olives became one of Jesus' most beloved places. He taught there. Prayed there. Rested there.
Yet the most significant moment happened in a garden at its foot.
Gethsemane.
The name comes from the Aramaic and Hebrew expression גת שמנים (Gat Shemanim), meaning "oil press."
An oil press was designed to crush olives until their oil flowed out.
That detail is not accidental.
Jesus entered a garden of crushing before He entered a cross of suffering.
Luke records something astonishing.
"Being in anguish, He prayed more earnestly, and His sweat was like drops of blood falling to the ground."
Luke 22:44
The Greek word used for anguish is ἀγωνία (agonia).
It is where we derive the English word agony.
It describes intense struggle.
Extreme emotional distress.
The battle of a soul carrying a weight beyond human comprehension.
Many people imagine Jesus calmly walking toward the cross without inner conflict.
The Scriptures reveal something far deeper.
The Son of God felt the full weight of what lay ahead.
The rejection.
The humiliation.
The torture.
The wrath against sin He would bear.
The separation He would experience.
The price of redemption.
Everything pressed down upon Him.
Like olives beneath a crushing stone.
Perhaps that is why so many of us can relate to Gethsemane.
Because life has its own presses.
The diagnosis we never expected.
The betrayal we never saw coming.
The marriage that shattered.
The child who walked away.
The addiction nobody knows about.
The anxiety hidden behind smiles.
The private battles fought after everyone else falls asleep.
Some readers know exactly what it feels like to be crushed.
To feel trapped between God's promises and your painful reality.
To wonder why heaven seems silent.
To ask questions you are almost afraid to pray.
Jesus understands that place.
Not theoretically.
Personally.
Hebrews 4:15 reminds us that we do not have a High Priest unable to sympathize with our weaknesses.
The Savior who redeemed us also experienced anguish.
The Savior who conquered death also felt sorrow.
The Savior who rose in victory also knelt in tears.
And that changes everything.
Because it means your suffering is not invisible.
Your tears are not ignored.
Your struggles are not forgotten.
The Mount of Olives teaches us something many believers desperately need to hear.
The crushing is not the end of the story.
The oil comes after the pressing.
The resurrection comes after the cross.
The dawn comes after the darkness.
Most people remember what happened at Calvary.
Far fewer remember what happened after the resurrection.
Acts 1 tells us Jesus returned once again to the Mount of Olives.
This time everything was different.
The cross was behind Him.
Death was defeated.
The tomb was empty.
The scars remained, but the suffering had accomplished its purpose.
Acts 1:9 records:
"He was taken up before their very eyes."
The Mount of Olives became the place of ascension.
The same mountain associated with agony became a mountain associated with glory.
The same location that witnessed sorrow witnessed triumph.
The same place that saw tears saw victory.
That is God's pattern throughout Scripture.
Joseph was sold before he ruled.
David was hunted before he was crowned.
Peter failed before he led.
Paul suffered before he transformed nations.
And Jesus was crucified before He was exalted.
The Kingdom often moves through valleys before reaching mountaintops.
Perhaps that is why so many people misunderstand their current season.
They assume the crushing means God has abandoned them.
The Mount of Olives reveals the opposite.
Sometimes the crushing is evidence that God is preparing something greater than we can yet see.
Romans 8:28 does not say everything is good.
It says God works all things together for good for those who love Him.
Even betrayal.
Even heartbreak.
Even failure.
Even scandal.
And nobody embodies that truth more completely than Jesus Himself.
Humanity's greatest scandal became heaven's greatest victory.
The cross was intended as public humiliation.
God transformed it into eternal redemption.
The instrument of shame became the symbol of salvation.
The place of death became the doorway to life.
That is what grace does.
Grace rewrites stories.
Grace rewrites futures.
Grace rewrites identities.
Grace rewrites destinies.
Grace takes what sin destroyed and rebuilds it through Christ.
Somebody reading this may feel disqualified because of mistakes.
You carry regret.
You carry shame.
You carry memories you wish could be erased.
You look at your past and see scandal.
Jesus looks at your future and sees redemption.
The Gospel is not the story of perfect people.
It is the story of a perfect Savior rescuing broken people.
That is why the Mount of Olives continues to speak across generations.
Its message is not merely historical.
It is personal.
Every believer eventually finds themselves in a Gethsemane.
Every believer eventually experiences a season of pressing.
Every believer eventually discovers that God's greatest work often happens in the places we would have chosen to avoid.
But if Jesus transformed the cross, He can transform your story.
If Jesus conquered death, He can conquer your despair.
If Jesus rewrote history, He can rewrite your future.
And perhaps that is the lesson I learned from the Mount of Olives.
God is never finished in the middle of the story.
What feels like the ending may simply be the beginning of redemption.
What feels like crushing may be preparation.
What feels like loss may become testimony.
What feels like scandal may become grace.
Because Jesus Christ still rewrites everything.
You never know whose Gethsemane season may be transformed by a reminder that God has not abandoned them.
Your testimony may become the encouragement someone else desperately needs today.
The mountain of crushing became the mountain of glory—and maybe God is doing the same thing with your story right now.
